PhD Dissertation Summary · Department of Computer Science, Yale University

Machine Learning Models that Connect Mind and World

Weikang Qiu Advisor: Prof. Rex Ying Committee: Smita Krishnaswamy, Arman Cohan, Yujun Yan (Dartmouth College)

Language has become the common interface between people and intelligent machines, yet putting a percept, an intention, or an intended movement into words can be slow, incomplete, or difficult. This dissertation develops machine learning methods for a more direct interface between mind and world, following a progression from brain signals, to semantics, to action. Four core studies each take one step along this progression.

Motivation

Language can be a narrow channel. Specifying a visual idea may take a long prompt listing objects, attributes and spatial relations, and some experiences, such as the structure and affective intensity of Kandinsky's Composition VII, can be perceived as a whole but are hard to state precisely in words. The same issue arises in the other direction, when a machine explains something to a person (Chapter 2). These limitations motivate a complementary channel through which percepts, intentions and internal states can be communicated without deliberate verbalization.

Three Challenges

Neural priors

Neural signals are high dimensional, and the useful relationships among brain regions are not specified in advance. Models must identify informative structure and incorporate it to improve prediction.

Addressed by HyBRiD; also the lateralization prior in MWM

Data and supervision

Brain recordings rarely come with semantic annotations of what a person perceives, knows or does, and collecting new annotated recordings is costly. Learning semantic representations that generalize across people requires deriving this supervision from other sources.

Addressed by MindLLM (annotations linked through stimulus images) and MWM (visual consequences as supervision)

Effective and efficient action

Translating intentions into physical action requires policies that remember relevant experience and respond promptly, even as inference over long observation histories grows costly.

Addressed by DySta
Chapter 2 · Prologue KDD Health Day 2025 · Best Paper

RepQA [1]Evaluating the Readability of Large Language Models in Patient Education Question Answering

PrologueMotivates Chapters 3–6

Before turning to the brain, the dissertation examines the language interface itself, in the direction from machine to person. RepQA asks whether LLMs can make patient-education answers easier to read without losing information. The consistent trade-off it finds shows that a language channel can lose information even when a capable model chooses the words, and it motivates the more direct interfaces between mind and world developed in the chapters that follow.

Motivation

Medical LLM benchmarks such as MedQA and PubMedQA measure factual or reasoning accuracy against professional examinations. In patient education, an answer is useful only if a lay reader can understand it, an axis these benchmarks largely overlook.

Method

RepQA contains 533 expert-grounded question–answer pairs curated from 27 authoritative sources and reviewed by nursing, public-health and clinical-communication professionals, plus 36,060 public-health questions for training. Answers are scored with three readability metrics (Flesch–Kincaid grade, professional-language proportion, Yngve depth) and an informativeness metric against the reference answer.

Contributions
  • A readability-centered benchmark and metric suite for lay-facing medical question answering.
  • An evaluation of 19 LLMs on following a requested reading level and recognizing the level a question or response requires.
  • A comparison of readability-control strategies: prompting, chain-of-thought, lookahead decoding, and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning (GRPO, DAPO).
Results

Readability gains are paid for in informativeness. Across readability control and RL fine-tuning (GRPO, DAPO), the grade levels removed track the information lost almost linearly (r = −0.96), and chain-of-thought loses more content than this rate (Figure 3). Even RL rewarding both accuracy and readability does not remove the trade-off. Models also shift readability in the requested direction but miss the absolute target level. For this dissertation, the trade-off is the motivating observation: what language drops between a machine and a person points to channels that do not depend on verbalization.

Chapter 3 ICML 2024 SignalsSemanticsActions

HyBRiD [2]Learning High-Order Relationships of Brain Regions

RepQA → HyBRiDSignals

RepQA showed how much a language interface can lose. We now turn to the neural signals that could support a more direct one. A first question is which neural priors, such as structural relationships among brain regions, improve how brain signals are modeled and predicted. HyBRiD answers it by learning which groups of regions jointly carry information about a cognitive outcome, as weighted hyperedges trained with an information-bottleneck objective.

Motivation

Cognition arises from interactions among many brain regions, yet standard fMRI biomarker methods score only pairwise connectivity. Prior high-order methods first enumerate or cluster candidate region sets and then select among them; since the space of region subsets is exponential, most informative combinations are never considered.

Method

Brain regions are nodes of a hypergraph. A Constructor with K heads learns one mask per hyperedge, shared across subjects, to select its member regions; a Weighter reads out each hyperedge's weight from its members' features, and a linear head predicts the phenotype. Training follows the maximally-informative, minimally-redundant criterion, max I(H;Y) − β·I(H;X). The prediction loss bounds the first term; for the intractable redundancy term, the multi-head drop-bottleneck gives a closed-form upper bound in the mask probabilities:

Proposition · multi-head drop-bottleneck
I(H;X) ≤ ∑k=1K I(𝒉k;X) ≤ ∑k=1K ∑i=1N I(𝒉ik;Xi) = ∑k=1K ∑i=1N ℍ[Xi] (1−pik)
Equality holds if and only if regions are independent and hyperedges do not overlap. Combined with the prediction loss, the training objective upper-bounds −I(H;Y) + β·I(H;X).
Contributions
  • Theory: the multi-head drop-bottleneck, a new information-bottleneck framework for identifying structures rather than compressing representations. Its proposition turns the intractable redundancy term into a closed-form bound that decomposes over hyperedges and regions, giving the MIMR objective a principled training loss.
  • End-to-end discovery of high-order brain relationships without enumerating candidates, at a cost of the same order as an MLP.
  • Subject-shared hyperedge structures with subject-specific weights, supporting consistent structures across people.
Results

ABCD (11,875 children; rest and three tasks at two timepoints) and ABIDE (three IQ targets), evaluated with connectome-based predictive modeling.

+12.1%average improvement over state-of-the-art predictive models on ABCD
+8.8%average improvement on ABIDE, best on every target
87%faster than the second-fastest deep learning baseline

Higher-degree hyperedges were more significant, and 60% of learned hyperedges remained significant even at p < 10−8, far exceeding pairwise edges.

Additional work · SWA [3] NeurIPS 2026

Small-World Allocation extends this structural perspective to artificial networks. It builds functional graphs over the attention heads of language models, and across six open-source models finds that higher small-world indices accompany lower answer-token loss on the DRE-Bench reasoning benchmark. Core and bridge scores derived from these graphs guide sparsity allocation across Transformer blocks and heads, improving pruned-model performance with SparseGPT and Wanda while better preserving small-world organization.

Chapter 4 ICML 2025 SignalsSemanticsActions

MindLLM [4]A Subject-Agnostic and Versatile Model for fMRI-to-Text Decoding

HyBRiD → MindLLMSignals → Semantics

HyBRiD identifies neural structures that are informative for one specified outcome. Yet the same brain activity supports many functions at once: perceiving a scene, retrieving memories and knowledge, processing language and symbols, and reasoning. MindLLM asks how one representation of fMRI can capture these multiple brain functions and make them readable as text across people. It pairs a subject-agnostic fMRI encoder with an LLM and trains it with brain instruction tuning over tasks organized by brain function.

Motivation

Existing fMRI-to-text decoders capture a narrow slice of what the brain encodes: they caption, or answer questions about, the image currently in view, leaving out functions such as memory, knowledge and symbolic processing. They are also subject-specific: each person's fMRI has a different number and layout of task-responsive voxels (12.7k–17.9k per subject in NSD), and pooling or sampling voxels to a fixed size loses spatial information.

Method

Neuroscience-informed attention: learnable queries attend over all voxels. Each voxel's key encodes where it is (a positional encoding of its coordinates plus embeddings from several brain parcellations), and its value is what it measures (the fMRI signal). The resulting fMRI tokens are prepended to instructions for a frozen LLM.

Brain Instruction Tuning (BIT): NSD's stimuli are COCO images, so existing COCO annotations can be paired with each recording. Tasks are selected and organized by the brain functions they engage: perception and scene understanding (captioning, visual QA), memory and knowledge retrieval (describing a previously seen image, knowledge-based QA), language and symbolic processing (text recognition, counting), and complex reasoning. The result is 980,610 conversations from 15 datasets.

Contributions
  • BIT, the first brain instruction-tuning dataset, organized by brain function so that one fMRI representation captures perception, memory and knowledge, language, and reasoning; it is built from existing annotations through the stimulus images, without additional scanning.
  • Neuroscience-informed attention that separates a voxel's functional identity (keys, largely shared across people) from its signal (values), giving one architecture for all subjects without pooling or subject-specific layers.
  • Multiple brain parcellations combined in the keys, instead of committing to a single atlas.
Results

Natural Scenes Dataset (8 subjects); comparisons with subject-specific and subject-agnostic decoders.

+12.0%average improvement over baselines across tasks spanning perception, memory and knowledge, language, and reasoning
+24.5%improvement in generalization to a held-out subject
+13.5%average improvement when adapting to new tasks, such as sentiment and affordance understanding

Training on multiple brain functions through BIT contributed a 28.0% average gain over training each task from scratch, and performance scaled with the number of training subjects for both seen and held-out subjects.

Additional work · PRISM and D-Edit

PRISM [5] ICLR 2026 · Oral compares language, vision and vision-language representation spaces for their alignment with fMRI. Caption-derived language-model embeddings aligned most strongly, motivating structured text descriptions of objects, attributes and relationships that guide object-centric diffusion for visual reconstruction, with up to 6% lower perceptual loss than prior methods on NSD, BOLD5000 and GOD.

D-Edit [6] AAAI 2025 enables object-level image editing by giving each item its own learned prompt and restricting interactions through grouped cross-attention. It improved source-image preservation and guidance consistency, and provides PRISM with a more expressive object-disentangled generator for structured descriptions.

Chapter 5 SignalsSemanticsActions

Mind World Models [7]Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics

MindLLM → MWMSemantics → Action

MindLLM connects brain signals to semantic content. MWM takes the next step from semantics to action: the visual consequences of behavior provide semantic supervision for learning action representations from motor EEG. EEG serves as the latent action of a world model, so learning to predict what happens next teaches the encoder what the action was, without action labels.

Motivation

Motor EEG decoders are trained on cue-based trials with coarse labels such as "left hand", which are costly to scale and ignore how a movement unfolds. EEG foundation models pretrain with EEG-only objectives that never supervise the link between neural activity and movement. Generic encoders also ignore lateralization: the same pattern signals a different acting side depending on the hemisphere.

Method

A mind model encodes EEG up to the current frame into a latent action. A world model, conditioned on that latent action, predicts the next frame's frozen DINOv2 features from the current frame. Because the EEG window ends at the current frame, the target is not already contained in the input. Training combines masked EEG reconstruction, EEG–frame contrastive alignment and future-feature prediction on 63 hours of synchronized EEG and egocentric video from 40 participants.

The Lateralization-Aware Transformer applies frame averaging over the original and hemisphere-mirrored inputs, producing a mirror-invariant bilateral component and a mirror-equivariant lateral component. When a video is flipped horizontally, only the lateral component is exchanged across hemispheres.

Contributions
  • Visual consequences as supervision for motor EEG: richer than categorical labels, free of action annotation, and scalable to naturalistic recordings.
  • A hemispheric prior built into the encoder through invariant and equivariant readouts, rather than learned from limited data.
  • A world model whose action interface transfers from EEG-derived to real actions, a path to world-model data without instrumented capture devices.
Results

Linear probes on 16 motor decoding tasks against EEG foundation models (BIOT, LaBraM, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE); world-model transfer with IMU signals as real actions.

+5.9%task-averaged balanced accuracy on 9 classification tasks
+16.2%task-averaged Pearson correlation on 7 regression tasks (force, kinematics, cursor velocity)
−23.2%L1 error in future prediction conditioned on real actions (−11.0% on held-out subjects)

The learned components behave as designed: the left- versus right-fist motor-imagery contrast is 81% mirror-antisymmetric in the lateral component, compared with 15% in the bilateral component.

Chapter 6 NeurIPS 2026 SignalsSemanticsActions

DySta [8]Static-Dynamic Disentanglement for Efficient Multi-Frame Vision-Language-Action Models

MWM → DyStaAction

MWM learns representations that support decoding action intentions from brain activity. DySta asks how machines can then translate human intentions into effective and efficient task execution. For robotic policies this requires memory of recent observations as well as fast inference, and DySta obtains both by separating the persistent and the changing parts of what the robot sees.

Motivation

Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the current frame, so a robot asked to press a button cannot tell whether it already has. Adding past frames multiplies hundreds of visual tokens per image, and large VLAs are already slow at each control step. Existing cache-reuse methods assume that visually unchanged patches keep stable latent representations, which does not hold inside Transformer backbones.

Method

Visual tokens are split into dynamic tokens and multi-level static tokens, with a contrastive loss that makes static tokens persistent within a trajectory. The context holds one copy of the static tokens plus dynamic tokens from several past steps. Placing static tokens first lets their key–value cache be reused across control steps, and a learned recache gate at each level decides when to refresh it.

Contributions
  • Static-dynamic disentanglement: one mechanism that provides both memory (compact multi-frame context) and speed (cache reuse).
  • A learned recache gate that replaces heuristic, pixel-similarity rules for deciding when to recompute.
  • LIBERO-Memory, a simulation benchmark of tasks in which the current frame alone is insufficient to choose the next action.
Results

Built on OpenVLA-OFT; SimplerEnv, LIBERO, LIBERO-Memory, and real-world tasks on a Cobot Magic robot.

2.26×inference speedup on SimplerEnv, with +3.9% success over the strongest baseline
2.21×real-world speedup, with +10.6% average success over the base model
+23.3 ptssuccess on real-world memory tasks (58.3% vs. 35.0%); +24.5% on LIBERO-Memory

On standard LIBERO, DySta raised average success from 95.4% to 96.0% while running 1.70× faster.

Additional work · PHIL [9] LoG 2022

A complementary way to realize an intention is to specify a target state and let the machine plan the intermediate steps. PHIL learns a search heuristic on graphs with given start and goal nodes, using a recurrent graph neural network with a compact memory of the explored graph. Across grid, citation, biological, syntax-tree and road-network benchmarks, it reduced visited nodes by 13.4% on average relative to the best baseline for each dataset, and supported efficient collision-free search in simulated indoor drone planning.

Chapter 7

Future DirectionsFrom reading brain activity to closed-loop intervention

The next step extends reading neural activity toward writing through stimulation. A multimodal brain world model would connect fMRI, EEG, MEG and functional ultrasound through a shared latent state and predict how that state evolves under a stimulus or stimulation, extending MWM's action-conditioned prediction from the external world to the brain itself. A control policy could then be learned on imagined trajectories in the Dreamer style, with decoded neural feedback guiding interventions. Closed-loop transcranial focused ultrasound for chronic pain is a motivating application.

Together, these studies advance neural prediction, semantic decoding, action-intention decoding and physical task execution along the progression from signals to semantics to action. They support the broader goal of human–machine symbiosis, in which intelligent systems extend people's ability to communicate, create and act in the world.
